summary: This document extends PCEP for Segment Routing with focus on SIDs and SR-Algorithms in traffic engineering. An SR-Algorithm sets the path computation algorithm. It updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603.

plainLanguage.summary: Each route label can say what rule picked its path, such as shortest or fastest. PCEP can now carry that information.

subtitle: How PCEP peers learn which routing algorithm each Segment Routing label belongs to, and how a path request can demand one.

tldr.problem: PCEP had no way to say which SR-Algorithm, the path computation algorithm used by the IGPs, goes with a segment identifier, or to ask a PCE to compute a path for a particular one.
tldr.mechanism: It adds an Algorithm field to SR-ERO, SRv6-ERO and the matching record route subobjects, a new SR-Algorithm TLV in the LSPA object, capability flags to negotiate it all, and new METRIC object types.
tldr.outcome: A PCE can follow IGP behavior, including Flexible Algorithms, and report full path information to a backup PCE. RFC 9933 updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603.

today: RFC 9933 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603, and no later RFC is listed as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) talk to a Path Computation Element (PCE), or one PCE talk to another. RFC 8664 and RFC 9603 extend it for Segment Routing (SR) over MPLS and IPv6 data planes.

This document extends PCEP for SR Traffic Engineering, focusing on Segment Identifiers (SIDs) and SR-Algorithms. An SR-Algorithm associated with a SID defines the path computation algorithm used by the IGPs. There are three extensions: signaling the SR-Algorithm in ERO and RRO subobjects, an SR-Algorithm constraint for path computation, and new METRIC object types. It updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603 to allow them.
sections.plainLanguage: Route labels in a network can follow different rules for picking a path. This paper lets the planning program and the routers talk about which rule is in use.

sections.title: Why the Extensions Are Needed
sections.content:
Existing PCEP specifications cannot explicitly signal or negotiate SR-Algorithm capabilities and constraints. Without an explicit algorithm, no constraint was implied, so SIDs with any SR-Algorithm could be used.

The main goal is to let a PCE use the path computation logic and topology information of the IGPs, including Flexible Algorithms. Paths then match the underlying routing behavior and can need fewer SIDs, and multi-domain Flexible Algorithm deployments become simpler to manage.

A PCE and a PCC may compute paths with different SR-Algorithms on their own, so the information must be exchanged for monitoring and troubleshooting. In high availability setups, a PCC that got a path from the primary PCE must report the full path, including the SR-Algorithm, to a backup PCE so that it can verify Prefix SIDs.

Putting the algorithm on each SID matters too. A Binding SID may have no algorithm, so claiming an entire path follows one algorithm can be wrong if it includes a Binding SID from another policy. Two IGP domains may also use the same Flexible Algorithm Definition under different algorithm numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: If a traveler only says "get me there", the planner cannot know whether you want the quickest or the cheapest way. Writing the rule on each step avoids mix-ups.

sections.title: Advertising Support
sections.content:
Support is announced with a new S (SR-Algorithm Capability) flag. In the SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV it is bit 5 and covers LSPs set up with PST 1 (Segment Routing). In the SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV it is bit 13 and covers PST 3 (SRv6). With S set to 0, behavior is as before.

The extensions MUST NOT be used unless both PCEP speakers set the S flag for the LSP's Path Setup Type. Otherwise the receiver MUST answer with a PCErr message with Error-Type 19 (Invalid Operation) and Error-value 33 (Attempted use of SR-Algorithm without advertised capability). A peer that gets an SR-ERO or SRv6-ERO subobject with the A flag set without the S flag advertised MUST treat the entire ERO as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the new feature, both sides must raise a hand to say they know it. If one did not, using it is an error.

sections.title: Algorithm in the ERO and RRO Subobjects
sections.content:
In the SR-ERO subobject (Type 36) a new A flag, when set, means a Subobject Extension Block is present. The block is variable length, always a multiple of 4 bytes and at least 4 bytes. Its first 4 bytes hold 24 unassigned bits (zero when sent, ignored on receipt) and an 8-bit Algorithm, taken from the IGP Algorithm Types registry. If A is the only extension flag set, the block length MUST be 4. Receivers MUST check that the Length, S bit, F bit, A bit and NT field agree; for example, with NT=1 and S=1 the Length must be 8 plus the block size. A mismatch makes the whole ERO invalid, answered with Error-Type 10 (Reception of an invalid object) and Error-value 11 (Malformed object).

The block is designed for growth. Future extensions define their own flag and capability signaling, and SHOULD use the unassigned bits first.

In the SRv6-ERO subobject (Type 40) the 8-bit Algorithm is carved out of the Reserved field, so the subobject length does not change. The SR-RRO and SRv6-RRO subobjects have the same format minus the L flag and may carry the same data.

If a PCC receives an Algorithm in a PCInitiate, PCUpd or PCRep message and includes that path in the ERO of a PCRpt, it MUST include the Algorithm value. When the SID is absent but the NAI and Algorithm are present, the PCC chooses the SID, and sends Error-Type 10 with Error-value 14 (Unknown SID) if it cannot find it in the SR-DB.
sections.plainLanguage: Each step on the route gets a small extra tag naming the rule behind it. A length check makes sure the tag was not cut off or padded wrongly.

sections.title: The SR-Algorithm Constraint
sections.content:
To ask a PCE to use a specific algorithm, the headend MUST put a new SR-Algorithm TLV (Type 66, Length 4) in the LSPA object. It is only for PST 1 or 3, and only its first instance is processed. It has a 16-bit Reserved field, 8 flag bits and an 8-bit Algorithm. The one defined flag, S (Strict), controls failure: if set, path computation MUST fail when the constraint cannot be met. If unset, the PCE MUST then try as if no SR-Algorithm constraint had been requested.

A PCC that gets the TLV in PCInitiate or PCUpd MUST echo it in the intended-attribute-list of a PCRpt. A PCE that gets it in PCRpt or PCReq MUST include it in the PCUpd or PCRep. A peer that did not advertise the S flag MUST ignore the TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a note on the trip request saying "use the fastest-route rule". A strict box says "if you cannot, say so", and a loose box says "then do your best".

sections.title: Computing Paths for an Algorithm
sections.content:
The PCE MUST NOT use Prefix SIDs of any SR-Algorithm other than the requested one. Protected Adjacency SIDs without an explicit algorithm are NOT RECOMMENDED, because the backup path may fail to forward over parts of the topology outside that algorithm. Binding SIDs are allowed, and a path Binding SID from another policy only if that policy's path meets all constraints of the current computation. If the PCE cannot find a path or does not support the constraints, it MUST return an empty ERO or a NO-PATH object.

The algorithm value picks the method. For values 0 to 127 the algorithm is a filter on which SIDs may be used, currently 0 (Shortest Path First) and 1 (Strict-SPF). An unsupported value in this range MUST be rejected with a PCErr of Error-Type 19 and Error-value 34 (Unsupported combination of constraints).

For values 128 to 255, the PCE MUST follow the IGP Flexible Algorithm procedures of RFC 9350, using topology data in its TED from IGPs or BGP-LS. It MUST optimize on the metric type in the Flexible Algorithm Definition and ignore the metric type sent by the PCC. The PCC MUST NOT put FAD constraints in its PCEP message, and the PCE SHOULD NOT include them in messages to the PCC. Extra constraints on top of the FAD may lengthen the SID list.
sections.plainLanguage: For simple rules the planner just skips labels that do not match. For custom rules, it rebuilds the map the way the routers do and finds the best path on that map.

sections.title: New METRIC Types
sections.content:
To support Flexible Algorithm metrics, the METRIC object gets new types, usable beyond Flexible Algorithms and with any PST. All values are IEEE floating point.

  • Path Min Delay (T=22): the sum of the minimum link delay of all links on a point-to-point path, in microseconds. P2MP Path Min Delay (T=23) is the worst delay among all tree destinations.
  • Path Bandwidth (T=24): the sum of the Bandwidth metric of the links on the path. P2MP Path Bandwidth (T=25) takes the worst among destinations. It is cumulative and differs from the BANDWIDTH object of RFC 5440.
  • User-defined (T=128 to 255): operator-assigned metrics for local use, matching the IGP Metric-Type registry values. For example, type 130 can represent the sum of the user-defined metric 130 along a path.

The processing rules for the METRIC object in RFC 5440 and RFC 8233 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The planner can now add up travel time, a capacity score, or a custom score you invent along the whole route, and judge routes by that total.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8253, RFC 8281, RFC 8664, RFC 9603 and RFC 9350 apply. Letting a PCE compute paths from Flexible Algorithm topology attributes adds exposures already known from IGP path computation. Securing the PCEP session with TLS is therefore RECOMMENDED, as in RFC 9325.

For operations, the feature MAY be enabled or disabled in global configuration and SHOULD be enabled by default. Implementations SHOULD let the operator view the capability, the FADs used and the nodes participating in the algorithm. The RFC defines no new liveness mechanism, and it inherits operational considerations from the IGP Flexible Algorithm documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The planner trusts the map it is given, so the conversation should be locked with TLS, and operators should be able to see which rules are in play.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: TLV type for the SR-Algorithm constraint.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Other flags are set to 0 and ignored.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Strict: path computation fails if the constraint cannot be satisfied.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: The SR-Algorithm to use in path computation.

items.label: Path Min Delay
items.desc: Sum of minimum link delay along a P2P path.

items.desc: Sum of the Bandwidth metric along a P2P path.

items.desc: Worst Bandwidth metric among tree destinations.
